thread.title: Deere's Q4: Gaining Traction By Combining Ag With Tech - Deere & Company (NYSE:DE)

author: DoctoRx
title: Deere's Q4: Gaining Traction By Combining Ag With Tech - Deere & Company (NYSE:DE)

organizations.name: combining ag with tech - deere & company

text:
Background John Deere, who moved west to escape creditors in New England, founded Deere ( DE ) in 1837. Imagine the year 2157 (not merely 2057), and if Apple ( AAPL ) remains in business and the industry leader, that would match DE's achievement. DE has thrived in one of the most difficult, cyclical industries around, vehicles for farmers. Panics, depressions, busts following booms, and never-ending competition have ensued. DE had a modest miss to consensus in Q4. But two major ag competitors, CNH Industrial ( CNHI ) - which is also a competitor to DE in the construction sector - and AGCO ( AGCO ) - each have greater profit margin and other pressures on them, based on my review of their latest earnings reports and conference calls. So does Caterpillar ( CAT ), a major competitor to DE's construction and forestry division.
Now, 181 years old, DE looks to up its game.
This article reports on DE's actions to build on its lead by going increasingly high tech. This process is underway and leads me to continue to both hold the stock despite both the Q4 miss and mildly disappointing guidance for FY 2019, and to look for opportunities to increase my holdings - but not at this time.
DE as a leader in its sectors I like to go with companies that the mythical Mr. Market prefers in times when the Fed is hostile and thus stressing out us long-side investors.
Traders have preferred DE's resilience in the current tough times for cyclicals; the chart compares DE to the above names as well as Kubota ( OTCPK:KUBTY ) and CAT:
DE data by YCharts Note : chart created intra-day Friday.
DE's 1-year outperformance is consistent with its relative performance since the ag market last peaked, as shown in a 5-year chart:
DE data by YCharts What I see in DE is focus and competence to explain its alpha relative to the industries in which it competes. DE shrank its shares outstanding substantially earlier in the decade when the stock was much cheaper. It sold the non-core OneSite business for the now-core Wirtgen road construction equipment business. After doing the Wirtgen deal, DE has put its focus both on operational integration and realization of synergies. It has also cut back sharply on capital return to shareholders while finances improve post-Wirtgen and while DE deals with spikes in its cost of goods.
However, I'm sitting tight with DE because I think there are...
Too many headwinds for now On Wednesday, DE released a detailed earnings report and held a conference call . A PDF presentation accompanied the call and is an important read.
DE initially sold off to $135 and below in pre-market trading, then surged to $145 or so early on, but prices were marked down by day's end. The reason was summarized by a Seeking Alpha post pre-market Wednesday:
Deere's 2019 outlook disappoints analysts
William Blair weighed in on Deere (NYSE: DE ) after earnings, saying 2019 guidance looks "somewhat conservative," and that continued material headwinds and light sales led to the quarterly miss. [More at link.]
As Blair noted, Q4 came in a little light to expectations for both product sales and earnings. Forward guidance was to $11+ for this fiscal year, also light to consensus.
Given the Fed is taking the punch bowl away, the global economy is decelerating, and DE had a miss-and-guide-down quarter, I see no reason to add shares.
But I did like a couple of points that DE made in its defense.
DE puts a couple of matters to bed The most important issue on the minds of traders has been the US trade war with China, and China's shift to purchase soybeans from Brazil and elsewhere. DE believes that this simply leads to the US sending its soy output elsewhere (AGCO said something similar on its conference call). DE also highlighted its success in Brazil in its presentation; it's making the case that trade-related trends are at least OK and maybe better than that for this company.
A second point that DE emphasized was that the Wirtgen deal is working out well. The acquisition completed last December. Wirtgen was a private, family-owned, family-run multinational German manufacturer of high-end road-building equipment. DE touted the deal as additive or possibly truly synergistic. With Wirtgen, DE now has a complete suite of road-building equipment. There are other benefits. Wirtgen was not US-focused, so DE gained more access to business out of the US while bringing Wirtgen to greater prominence in the US.
DE reported Wednesday that Wirtgen, in its third full quarter under the DE umbrella, was performing at the high end of expectations. DE sees its synergy goals being achieved. Thus, it's a "so far, so good" story that diminishes the omnipresent concern that a family is selling out to an American multinational because the business has problems.
The biggest news for many DE-watchers was a complete surprise, though forward-looking and aspirational rather than proven:
DE aims for a big increase in profitability DE's CFO completed the prepared remarks in the conference call by saying:
Second, in our recent review of the John Deere strategy, we revised our 2022 financial aspirations to reflect our higher expectations for the business. As a result, we raised our mid-cycle operating margin target from 12% to 15%...
The first question often addresses the big surprise in a company's earnings report or prepared remarks. This part of the first question stood out for me:
I don't think [DE] has ever hit that [15% margin]... in the past.
The CFO, Raj Kalathur, made several points in explanation.
1. He pointed to DE's precision ag and other technology investments, which go back to investments made in the 1990s. He asserted that these provide significant and differentiated value to customers, saving them money, thus allowing DE to share in that saving via higher profit margins. The last questioner provided support for this, saying:
So the feedback from our dealer survey last week, the dealers gathering $2000 to $3000 of annual subscription revenue from customers if not more on a cumulative basis from all of your various precision ag technologies... Is it unreasonable to think that precision ag is a $500 million revenue business for Deere today, if not larger at substantially higher margins than the rest of the company?
DE would not answer that directly, saying:
... we think [precision ag is] a significant opportunity to create value for customers and we think as we do that we're going to be able to participate in that value.
So we see that at least one brokerage (BofA/ML) is finding DE gaining traction and enhanced margins with precision ag and related technologies despite relatively weak business conditions on the US farm.
2. The second point the CFO made was also technological, and relates to DE's strong dealer network:
... Connected Support; these type of technologies that we are incorporating now will help us develop a much higher share of the aftermarket business going forward.
Note that while this second point relates mostly to strengthening DE's dealers, other aspects of DE's technologies include connectivity that tie into precision ag that is built into the machine that DE sells to its dealers.
3. The third point Mr. Kalathur made reiterated the Wirtgen upside:
... the synergies from Wirtgen both on the cost side and the sales side and some of the growth prospects there will also allow us to improve our margins.
4 and 5. The CFO's final points include cost reductions in DE's manufacturing, by various means, such as going more digital, using robots, and reducing the cost of materials.
John Lagemann , a senior VP at DE, gave an extended presentation of these and other matters in his prepared remarks. There is a lot in them - covering more than just the rationale for DE's goal of higher margins.
Next, I would like to hone in just a bit on precision ag, DE's focus on it, and DE's case that it is already bringing the company tangible competitive benefits.
Precision ag and other technologies: bringing DE to greater success? For the current FY 2019, DE is forecasting about 5% sales growth ex-forex, ahead of the projected ag industry growth, which it presents in local currencies by region. (See slides 11-12 for its forecast for the industry and then its own forecast.)
In the presentation, DE references ExactEmerge and ExactApply as two of its precision ag technologies. The first is a seed planting technology; the latter relates to sprayers.
Important : DE has sued AGCO for patent infringement over a set of Monsanto products that AGCO acquired last year, Precision Planting, which competes with ExactEmerge. There could be upside to DE should it prevail. I do not believe that AGCO is counter-suing.
DE discusses the above products in only limited fashion on its web site. Mostly it wants farmers to get interested enough to see their John Deere dealer and get educated, i.e. receive a sales pitch.
A good overview for investors comes from a DE web page titled, simply, Precision Ag Technology . This lists several points related to DE's offerings. The first two set a certain tone, making DE sound like a Silicon Valley player:
Data Management Improve application rates, fuel economy, input placement, and land stewardship with John Deere displays and StarFire™ receivers. This well-supported precision technology can be put to work quickly so you'll get fast results -- and a fast payback.
Remote Management See how your machines are performing and how jobs are progressing, anytime or anywhere.
Farther down the page, after actually referring to the nuts and bolts of farming, DE returns to this theme, saying:
Only John Deere seamlessly connects people, equipment, and technology to give you an advantage. “Anybody that we partner with, if they have questions, they don't have to call me. They can go log in and it’s there. And it's effortless.”
The above verbiage could come from Cisco Systems ( CSCO ) or Microsoft ( MSFT ).
The next panel is similar:
The farming productivity of tomorrow is at your fingertips today.
Operations Center lets you collect, access, analyze, and share data…on your computer, tablet, or phone ...from your office, truck, or fields. One look tells you where all your equipment and people are... You can even view your machine’s displays remotely. Collect data across the full growing season, and use it to make better decisions. It's like Air Traffic Control for your farm operation.
A different web page , also titled Precision Ag Technology, gets us more to product offerings that are actual products rather than tech. Since I know nothing about farming, I'll stop here on this topic.
All the above ties into DE's industry-leading R&D budget, which is high as a percentage not of sales but of profits. Included in my view of DE's strong R&D effort are various bolt-on acquisitions, plus partnerships with smaller innovator companies.
Technology exists to be applied to improve production of existing goods and services, and to enable new ones. I like to see DE doing that on the oldest type of "manufacturing" site known to man, the farm.
Now it's time to tie the above threads together to give my thoughts on DE as an investment.
Summary - an open field may lie ahead, but obstacles exist straight ahead DE is guiding to about $11+ EPS for FY 2019, which ends at the end of October 2019. At Friday's closing price of $142.84, that puts DE around 13X current-year projected GAAP EPS. That compares with S&P's consensus projected GAAP EPS for the 12 months ending 9/30/19 of $154.42; with the S&P 500 ( SPY ) closing Friday at 2633, the SPY has a 17.0X forward P/E. Thus DE is at almost a 25% discount to the market. I think that's fair.
DE said in the conference call that North American ag, its single most important market, has not even yet reached mid-cycle, but offsetting that is that construction may be at its peak in the US and elsewhere. Thus, perhaps the 13X forward P/E is a mid-cycle P/E for DE, versus a high late-cycle P/E for the SPY. But no one knows except in retrospect.
Looking to the future, DE has enough credibility with me to expect it to move toward its margin goals. DE's construction division will learn from Wirtgen to improve sales and margins; precision ag plus connectivity (i.e. tech) will do the same for DE's dominant ag segment. Those are the goals, along with improved manufacturing margins. If successful, that would almost certainly lead to DE having a higher relative P/E, both to the SPY and to its competitors.
DE has seen very little insider selling. That's important to me given that many managements running a faltering business are tempted to announce grandiose goals while they sell out as close to the top as possible.
In summary, I see competing offsets to the DE investment case. The Fed has raised the cost of borrowing for DE's customers, and the Fed has also been decreasing liquidity. So, as I said above and have said previously, that makes all risk assets a difficult 'buy' for yours truly. That's especially so for DE given the miss in Q4 and somewhat weak guidance. But in the here and now of the stock market, DE is being given a relative vote of confidence by Mr. Market; anxiety over the trade issues with China may have been overdone with regard to ag machinery companies; DE appears to be gaining profitable share over other ag competitors; and the company has gone very public with its plan to up its game throughout the company. Thus I see no reason to sell, and look forward to tracking DE's progress in the months and years ahead. It may be drizzling on DE right now, but there could be a bright open field ahead for the company and its shareholders. Here's hoping!
Thanks for reading and sharing any thoughts and knowledge you may have on DE and its markets.
Disclosure: I am/we are long DE,CSCO,MSFT.
